verdict.root_cause: checkoutservice is not itself broken: no recorded deploy, config or endpoint change over the full 24h window [tr_a6957e4bcc31][tr_799a128029f1], the process stays alive and keeps accepting traffic, and it emits no error or warn lines at all [tr_3d794d53052e]. What changed is what happens after a request arrives — early in the window every PlaceOrder line is followed by payment confirmation, confirmation email and a message write, while from ~18:07 onward only the order-entry line appears [tr_3d794d53052e]. Requests begin and then hang before the first downstream step that logs a result, and a fraction surface as errors: span error ratio rose from ~1.2% baseline to ~11.7% mean with a ~29% peak, first crossing at 17:45, ~22 minutes before the alert [tr_dcd49902d604]. Errors are partial and intermittent, the signature of timeouts against a slow dependency. productcatalogservice is excluded (identically zero error ratio across 133 samples, working collector) [tr_ef47f2d347e2]. The payment call is the first downstream hop whose completion is logged, and it is exactly that line that disappears, so the most probable failing element is paymentservice becoming slow enough that checkout requests block and a fraction time out. Its only recorded changes are a routine automated telemetry-endpoint set/revert, fully reverted 48 minutes before onset with net state unchanged [tr_c95aab5ae90c], so this is latency in the dependency, not a wrong config value.
verdict.reasoning: The mechanism is waiting, not crashing: checkoutservice serves and logs inbound requests to the end of the window with no errors of its own, so the failure is silent inside a call it makes [tr_3d794d53052e]. The truncated log sequence across multiple currency values locates the stall at a downstream hop rather than in checkout's own handling. The partial, oscillating error curve with onset 22 minutes before the alert fits a timeout budget being exceeded on a fraction of requests [tr_dcd49902d604]. Change history removes deploy and config explanations at both ends [tr_a6957e4bcc31][tr_799a128029f1][tr_c95aab5ae90c], and productcatalogservice is affirmatively cleared [tr_ef47f2d347e2]. Naming paymentservice is inferential: it rests on the payment confirmation being the first downstream completion checkout logs and the first to vanish.
open_questions: paymentservice was never measured — no latency, error, saturation or log dispatch ran against it; only its change history was queried.
No latency data was returned for any service; every metrics dispatch evaluated only the error-ratio template [tr_dcd49902d604][tr_ef47f2d347e2].

cartservice and shippingservice have no samples in either window [tr_410a7fdf9e8d][tr_00ae781e435a], so they are neither implicated nor cleared; emailservice and the message-broker hop were never dispatched at all.

alternatives.root_cause: A downstream hop other than payment — emailservice, the message-write/broker path, or an untelemetered cartservice/shippingservice call — is the slow dependency stalling checkout requests.
alternatives.why_not: The payment confirmation is the earliest downstream completion line to disappear [tr_3d794d53052e], so a later hop would not suppress it; but these services were never measured [tr_410a7fdf9e8d][tr_00ae781e435a], so this remains open.

alternatives.root_cause: checkoutservice itself exhausted a local resource — connection pool slots, threads or file descriptors — so requests queue after entry and never reach the payment call.
alternatives.why_not: No saturation or latency metrics were collected for checkoutservice [tr_dcd49902d604], and pool exhaustion is usually secondary to a slow downstream holding connections open; the intermittent partial error pattern fits timeouts better than hard resource starvation.

proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no effect is expected. The reason is that the only candidate action (restart_service on paymentservice) rests on a dependency that was never measured: no latency, error-ratio, saturation or log query was ever dispatched against paymentservice, only its change history [tr_c95aab5ae90c]. The inference that paymentservice is slow is drawn entirely from a negative signal on checkoutservice — the disappearance of the 'payment went through' log line after ~18:07 while order-entry lines continue [tr_3d794d53052e] — plus an error ratio that rose from ~1.2% to ~11.7% with onset at 17:45 [tr_dcd49902d604]. That pattern is equally consistent with a stall at emailservice, the message-broker write, cartservice or shippingservice (the latter two have zero samples in both windows and are neither implicated nor cleared), or with checkoutservice blocking on a call whose result it simply never logs. Before any action, the gap that must close is one metric_baseline or log query against paymentservice covering 17:30-18:15: if its request-duration p95 or p99 climbs at or just before 17:45, the restart becomes proposable; if it is flat, the mechanism is elsewhere.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if a latency or saturation measurement on paymentservice, once taken, shows a clear p95/p99 climb beginning at or before 17:45 that matches the checkoutservice error onset — in that case the delay cost real orders. It is also wrong if paymentservice logs show a stuck worker pool, connection-pool exhaustion or a hung goroutine, i.e. genuine process state, which is the precondition restart_service actually needs. Note also that even the proposed action's success would be hard to read: with no pre-existing paymentservice latency series, 'latency recovered' could not be measured, only the indirect proxies of checkoutservice error ratio falling back toward ~1.2% and the payment-confirmation log line resuming.
proposal.risk: Restarting paymentservice on this evidence would discard in-flight payment attempts and any in-process state at the exact moment a fraction of checkout requests are already hanging mid-transaction, converting silent stalls into hard failures for those users. If the true stall is downstream of payment (email, message write) or in a service with no telemetry at all (cartservice, shippingservice), the restart changes nothing, consumes the incident's attention, and produces a false negative that pushes the investigation away from the real dependency. restart_service is also marked non-reversible: if paymentservice fails to come back cleanly, checkout goes from ~11.7% errors to a total order-placement outage.
proposal.blast_radius: A restart of paymentservice would be seen by checkoutservice (its caller in this graph), and through it by frontend and loadgenerator, which are already alerted; the connection reset would appear as a brief spike in checkoutservice errors above the current ~29% peak before any recovery. Abstaining has zero blast radius: the incident continues in its present state, with checkoutservice accepting traffic and roughly 88% of requests still succeeding [tr_dcd49902d604], while the paymentservice measurement is taken.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical alert on checkoutservice followed by the load generator indicates real user-facing order failures, not a quiet warning. No open incidents to attribute it to, and the alerts alone don't distinguish a bad deploy from a failing downstream dependency.
